name: EVERYTHING EVERYWHERE ALL AT QUINCE BURGER

recipe.history:
The quince is among the most ancient and storied fruits of the Mediterranean and Middle Eastern worlds, cultivated for at least four thousand years across the arc of land stretching from Persia through the Caucasus into Greece and the Iberian Peninsula. The golden, fragrant fruit that Aphrodite holds in countless ancient Greek sculptures and paintings is almost certainly a quince, not an apple — its divine associations and its perfumed, intoxicating aroma made it the fruit of love and beauty in the ancient world. The Romans made a sweet quince preparation called melomeli, preserved in honey, and spread the cultivation of quince throughout their empire. In medieval Europe, quince marmalade — the original marmalade, from the Portuguese marmelo, meaning quince — was a luxury of the wealthy, a dense, ruby-red sweetmeat that required hours of cooking to transform the hard, astringent raw fruit into something transcendent. Spain and Portugal developed a deep culinary tradition with quince, producing membrillo (quince paste) that remains today one of the great cheese accompaniments in the world.

Quince arrived in the Americas with early European colonists and was widely grown in colonial American gardens, though it fell from fashion as easier-to-eat apples and pears came to dominate the orchard. It persisted in traditional American farmhouse cooking — quince preserves, quince jelly, quince butter — until the late twentieth century, when the food renaissance began to restore interest in heirloom and forgotten ingredients. The craft condiment movement embraced quince paste (membrillo) as a sophisticated accompaniment, and its application on burgers grew naturally from the charcuterie board tradition of pairing membrillo with aged cheese. A quince jelly glaze on a beef patty creates a mahogany-lacquered surface of extraordinary beauty and a sweet-tart depth of flavor that no other fruit quite replicates. It is a burger that feels simultaneously ancient and contemporary — like it has arrived from every direction at once.

I first encountered quince as an ingredient through a jar of membrillo my grandmother kept in her pantry, reserved for special occasions and served in thin slices alongside manchego cheese. The flavor hit me like a memory I had never experienced — simultaneously familiar and utterly strange, floral and tart and deeply sweet all at once. Years later, when I made a quince jelly glaze for a burger, I was trying to recapture something of that memory. I cooked the quince paste down with a splash of red wine vinegar and a knob of butter until it became a glossy, shimmering glaze, and I brushed it over the patty in the final minute of cooking. The burger emerged from the pan lacquered with a deep amber-red glaze that smelled like autumn and ancient orchards. On top of that, a smear of quince jelly on the bun, some aged manchego melted over the patty, and a handful of bitter watercress. It was a burger that tasted like it had been everywhere and arrived at this moment from all directions simultaneously.

The case for medium rare begins and ends with the texture of properly cooked beef — that yielding, slightly resistant give of muscle fiber that has been brought to exactly the right temperature and no further. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the patty is the ideal vessel for the quince glaze: hot enough to caramelize the glaze's sugars in the final cooking seconds, moist enough to keep the glaze from becoming brittle and sticky, and rich enough in fat to balance the glaze's acidity. A well-done patty would char the quince glaze to bitterness and present nothing beneath it but dry, gray disappointment. Medium rare is the temperature at which this burger fulfills its potential — ancient fruit meeting contemporary technique at the precise point where they make each other better.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 lbs fresh quince (about 3 large), peeled, cored, and chopped
4 tbsp quince paste (from above, or store-bought membrillo)
6 slices aged Manchego cheese (or young Manchego if preferred)
Dijon mustard (for spreading on bun top)
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with 1 tsp sugar; rest 5–10 minutes until foamy. Combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt in a stand mixer. Add yeast mixture and 2 eggs; mix on medium. Add butter tablespoon by tablespoon. Knead 8 minutes until smooth. Refrigerate overnight in an oiled, covered bowl.
2. Remove dough, divide into 6 portions, shape into tight rounds, and proof on a lined baking sheet for 2–3 hours until doubled. Brush with egg wash, bake at 375°F for 16–18 minutes. Cool completely.

3. Make the quince paste: Combine chopped quince, sugar, water, and lemon juice in a heavy-bottomed saucepan. Cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, until quince is completely soft, about 30 minutes. Use an immersion blender or transfer to a blender and purée until smooth. Return purée to pan and cook over low heat, stirring constantly, until the paste is very thick, deep rose-colored, and pulls away from the sides of the pan, 30–45 more minutes. Pour into a parchment-lined loaf pan and let cool completely to set. Refrigerate; it will firm up as it cools.

4. Make the quince jelly glaze: Combine 4 tbsp quince paste, red wine vinegar, butter, water, and a pinch of salt in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Stir until paste melts and mixture forms a smooth, glossy glaze. Keep warm over very low heat.
5. Prepare the patties: Form ground beef into 6 patties (about 4 oz each), 3/4 inch thick with a center dimple. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add oil. Sear patties dimple-side up for 3 minutes until a deep crust forms. Flip and place a slice of Manchego on each patty. Cook 2 minutes, then brush the top of each patty generously with warm quince jelly glaze. Cook 30–60 more seconds until glaze caramelizes slightly and internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3–4 minutes, tented with foil.
7. Toss watercress with olive oil, sherry vinegar, and a pinch of flaky salt.
8. Toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet 1–2 minutes until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread a thin layer of quince paste on the bottom bun and a thin smear of Dijon mustard on the top bun. Place the glazed, Manchego-topped patty on the bottom bun. Pile dressed watercress on top. Crown with the top bun and serve immediately.
